definition.text: A budget constraint is the full set of combinations of goods and services a person can afford with their income at current prices.

facts.text: With two goods it is a straight line, the budget line, showing the trade-off between them.
The slope of the budget line is the price ratio of the two goods, which is the opportunity cost of one more unit of one good in units of the other.
Together with indifference curves, the budget constraint is the basic tool for analysing consumer choice.
The best affordable bundle usually lies where an indifference curve just touches the budget line.
Taxes, subsidies, quantity discounts and welfare benefits can make budget constraints kinked or non-linear.
In labour economics, the wage acts as the price of leisure: one more hour of leisure costs one hour's wage.

definition.text: An intertemporal budget constraint links what a person can consume in different periods through borrowing and saving at an interest rate.

facts.text: Borrowing now raises present consumption at the cost of less consumption later, while saving does the reverse.
Behavioural economics adds present bias, in which people give extra weight to consumption now over consumption later.

definition.text: A soft budget constraint exists when an organisation expects an outside body, usually a government, to cover its losses if it gets into financial trouble.

facts.text: Hungarian economist János Kornai introduced the term in the late 1970s to study state-owned firms in centrally planned economies.
Expecting bailouts, such firms invested too much, saved too little on costs and lobbied for more resources, contributing to chronic shortages.
The expectation of rescue creates moral hazard, as with too-big-to-fail banks.

definition.text: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'other things being equal', used to study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same.

facts.text: A standard example: if the price of milk falls, ceteris paribus, people will buy more milk.
The clause does not claim nothing else changes; it isolates the effect of one change.
Alfred Marshall popularised it in the 19th century, describing it as a 'pound' where disturbing causes are set aside for a time.
Because economic variables can only be isolated in theory, ceteris paribus can only reveal tendencies, not absolutes.
Marshall warned that the narrower the question, the less closely it matches real life, as in assuming hydrocarbon fuels are infinite.
In highly interconnected systems, changing one variable changes all the others, so holding everything else constant is not possible in reality.

title: Comparative advantage

definition.text: Comparative advantage is the principle that people, firms and countries can gain from trade even when one of them is better at producing everything.

facts.text: Gains are greatest when each party specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trades for the rest.
It differs from absolute advantage, which is about being more productive overall.
David Ricardo developed the classical theory in 1817, using the example of Portugal and England producing wine and cloth.
Ricardo's theory emerged in the debate over Britain's 1815 Corn Laws, which taxed imported grain to protect landowners.
In 1930 Gottfried Haberler restated the idea in terms of opportunity cost, measuring a good's value in forgone units of another good.
It describes the benefits specialisation and trade would bring, not a strict prediction of actual behaviour.
Critics such as James K. Galbraith argue that countries locked into agriculture stay poor because farming depends on land, a finite resource.

contested_note: Some economists dispute that comparative advantage justifies free trade, pointing to strategic trade policy and global value chains.

definition.text: Compensating variation is the amount of money that would leave a person exactly as well off after a price change as before, measured at the new prices.

facts.text: John Hicks introduced the measure in 1939.
It can be read as what a planner must pay to compensate a consumer for a price change after it happens.
It underlies Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: a policy passes if winners could compensate losers, even if they do not.
When a price change has no income effect, compensating variation equals equivalent variation and both equal the change in consumer surplus.
